findings.title: why_unclear misses second readings that come from incoming ticket links and body mentions. These exist only in the 5,000-document bank, so they mix into the size comparison
findings.evidence: questions()/units() look only at outgoing structured fields: ticket_link uses the from-ticket's dependencies, parent_issue, sub_issues and linked_issues; pr_issue and issue_pr_author use only linked_linear. The bank also stores the reverse of every reference (bank.py:166-171 adds 'referenced_by' on the target, and the planner follows it), and it records ticket keys cited in a document's body as 'mentions_key' refs (sources.py:325). So 'Ticket K is linked to another ticket. What status is that other ticket in?' has a second answer whenever another ticket in the set lists K in its dependencies or parent_issue. I counted this over four throwaway draws (seeds 997, 101, 202, 303, question seed = seed+1, order-test wordings), with the 50 picked as build_sets does. Kept ticket_link questions with such an incoming link: 4/40, 2/19, 0/40 and 4/36, and the other ticket's status or assignee differed in 4, 1, 0 and 4 of them. Picked ticket_link questions affected: 1, 1, 0 and 0 of 7, each with a different value. Seed 997 also had 1 of 12 kept issue_pr_author questions where a second PR in the set cites K, and 2 of 18 kept pr_issue questions where the PR body cites another ticket in the set (ENG-4821, ENG-7019 as mentions_key). In the pool, 1 of the 56 plantable PRs lists a linked_jira key that has a Jira document; draw() does not block that Jira document, so 'the ticket linked to PR #n' could then have a Jira answer. The other ticket is normally not a gold document, so it is absent from the small bank. not_reproduced passes these questions because the generator's answer does reproduce there. Any error the second reading causes therefore counts as a size effect in rules 1, 4 and 5.
findings.fix: Extend why_unclear with a 'linked' reason, or fold it into 'named'. Flag ticket_link when another Linear or Jira document in the set lists K in a link field and its asked field differs from the expected value. Flag issue_pr_author when another PR in the set cites K in any field the bank reads as a reference (SourceDoc.refs, including mentions_key). Flag pr_issue when the PR cites another ticket in the set, through linked_jira or its body, whose asked field differs. Alternatively, in draw(), skip the Jira document linked by a planted PR. Report the count with the other reasons and add the reason to the pre-registration's list.

verdict.reason:
The main claim holds. Some sub-claims do not.

Confirmed:
- why_unclear (cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_5k.py) never looks at incoming links.
- The bank adds a 'referenced_by' fact on the target ticket for every structured reference field of the citing document (bank.py:166-171, resolved to the target document by resolve()). The planner follows it: NOT_LINKS is only {"from_document"}.
- I reproduced the counts on throwaway draws: seed 101 had 2 of 19 kept ticket_link questions with an incoming Linear link, and 1 picked; seed 202 had 0 of 40; seed 997 had 4 of 40 (incoming dependencies or parent_issue), and 1 picked.
- not_reproduced passes all of them.
- I built 5,000-document and small v2 banks for 11 of these questions (inlink/ under rev5ka) and ran v9 and v13. The referenced_by plan shows up as a competing plan only at 5,000. In the two picked cases (seed 101 ticket_link-assignee-069, seed 997 ticket_link-assignee-169), v13 still took the outgoing 'dependencies' path and was right.
- The plan does change in one case: seed 997 ticket_link-status-103, a kept question (DES-912 links to DES-913, and DES-913 links back). On the small bank v13 answers through referenced_by and is right for the right reason (rests_on=True). At 5,000, PM-7644, which is not a gold document, also lists DES-912 in its dependencies. The referenced_by hop then reaches two tickets with different statuses and returns nothing. v13 falls back to DES-912's own status, 'Done', which matches the expected 'Done' only by chance. So rests_on=False at 5,000: rule 5 counts it as lost to size. If the own status had differed, rules 1 and 4 would count it too.
- The other ticket is a second right answer, because K is linked to J. The pre-registration says such questions are set aside, but why_unclear does not do this.

Not confirmed:
- The mentions_key and body-mention parts. The fact bank never reads SourceDoc.refs. Body keys become only text_key facts with no value_entity, and the planner skips text_ fields. So a PR body citing K or another ticket gives the system no second path.
- In the draws I checked, no second PR referenced K through a structured field. The issue_pr_author and pr_issue body cases are therefore only semantic.
- The planted-PR linked_jira case needs that PR to be planted (10 of 56) and its Jira document to be drawn. That is unlikely.

Size of the effect: about 0 to 1 affected picked ticket_link question per draw. One question is worth about 0.015-0.02 of the mean. The ticket_link part should get a 'linked' set-aside reason (or the cases should be counted) before the draw is frozen.

findings.title: 'Jira tickets have no due date' is not true of the data: ticket_reading reads only due_date and ignores Jira SLA due dates
findings.evidence: Of the 3,588 remaining Jira documents, 2,751 have sla_due_at and 2,170 have first_response_due_at. Only 1 (INT-33210) has due_date. ticket_reading's person_first branch sorts by _iso(raw['due_date']), so under the Linear-and-Jira reading of 'Of all the tickets assigned to {p}, which one is due first?' a Jira ticket's SLA due date never counts. The pre-registration nevertheless calls that reading legitimate and says person_first 'never changes'. In throwaway draws (997, 101, 202), 3, 1 and 1 kept person_first questions had the person holding a Jira ticket whose sla_due_at is earlier than the expected first Linear due date. None of those happened to be among the 7 picked.
findings.fix: Pick one and pre-register it: (a) treat sla_due_at as a due date in ticket_reading for person_first and set those questions aside as 'tickets'; or (b) state in the pre-registration that SLA and first-response deadlines are not due dates, and correct the sentence 'Jira tickets have no due date'.

verdict.reason: The data claims hold, but no test number depends on them. Checked against the remaining pool (15 earlier folders excluded): of the 3,588 Jira documents, 2,751 have sla_due_at, 2,170 have first_response_due_at, and only 1 has due_date (INT-33210, 2026-03-22). So the sentence in docs/FACTBANK_5K_PREREGISTRATION.md that "Jira tickets have no due date" is not accurate. It is literally false for that one ticket, which ticket_reading does handle because it reads due_date for Jira too. It is arguable for SLA deadlines. understand.json makes the same assumption ("person_first is unaffected because the Jira records have no due_date"). I re-ran throwaway draws 101, 997 and 202 with draw(), questions(), why_unclear() and pick(), writing only under rev5ka/. They reproduce the finding: 1, 3 and 1 kept person_first questions (out of 24, 38 and 26) where the person has a Jira ticket whose sla_due_at is earlier than the expected Linear due date. None of them was among the 7 picked. The finding does not affect the test, though. I built a 93-document bank from those three draws: each of the 23 person_first questions whose person holds a Jira ticket, with those people's Linear and Jira documents. The bank does hold sla_due_at facts (22) and first_response_due_at facts (16). I asked v4, v8, v9, v11 and v13. Every person_first plan read due_date, which is also the field the expected answers use. No arm ever answered with a Jira key, including on the 5 questions where the Jira SLA date is earlier. Two v13 answers were wrong, but both are expected-answer changes: those two people appear in two of the draws, so the merged bank holds Linear issues the original questions never saw. Both answers are still Linear keys read from due_date. The code agrees with this. engine.CUES maps "due" and "deadline" only to due_date, and reader.FORM_FIELD maps "due date" only to due_date, which covers the v12/v14 form. On the seen mt5k probe at 5,000 documents, v13 scored 8/8 on person_first. So the second reading only exists as a human interpretation of the question, and none of the arms tested gives that answer. The expected answers, what is set aside, the scores, the rules and the fairness between arms are all unchanged. The fix is a wording correction to the pre-registration (option b), not a code change.

findings.title: draw() does not screen tracker keys that are not plain keys: possible unscoreable expected ids and a crash in not_reproduced
findings.evidence: 32 remaining tracker documents (29 Linear, 3 Jira) have a key field that does not fullmatch KEY. Examples: 'ENG-642317-decision-mesh-schema-refactor', 'ENG-60412-prefix-aware-...', 'PM-31415927', 'PM-314159265'. _key deduplicates on the whole uppercased string, so 'ENG-642317-DECISION-...' and a plain 'ENG-642317' are treated as different keys and both can be drawn. questions() builds expected ids from the whole string, while ids_in('ENG-642317-DECISION-MESH-SCHEMA-REFACTOR', 'key') returns {'ENG-642317'}, so such an id can never be matched in an answer. For a compare_two pair that names an 8- or 9-digit key, KEY.findall returns one key, and `a, b = KEY.findall(q['question'])[:2]` in not_reproduced raises ValueError (I checked this directly), which would abort build_sets. The risk per draw is small: seed 101 drew one such document (ENG-48291-SERVICE-ERROR-...), and no question named it.
findings.fix: In draw(), skip tracker documents whose key does not fullmatch KEY and count them under a new reason such as skipped['key not a plain ticket key']. Alternatively, in not_reproduced, guard the unpacking and treat a compare question with fewer than two keys found as not reproduced.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. Every part of the mechanism shows up in the real code and data.

**The odd keys exist.** The remaining pool (306,471 documents after excluding the 15 folders in the run script) holds 32 tracker documents whose key does not fullmatch KEY: 29 Linear and 3 Jira. Four of the Linear ones have 8- or 9-digit keys and due dates: PM-31415927, PM-10000000, PM-314159265 and PM-31415926. Several odd keys also have a plain twin in the pool. For example, plain ENG-314159 is on 64 documents. `_key` dedups on the whole uppercased string, so draw() can take both the odd document and one plain twin.

**The crash happens.** I ran `questions()` on a real two-document set: the PM-31415927 Linear document plus one plain dated Linear document. It produced "ENG-3927 vs PM-31415927 - which one's due first?". `why_unclear` kept the question and `pick` picked it. `not_reproduced` then raised `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)` at `a, b = KEY.findall(q["question"])[:2]` (factbank_5k.py:263). That error would abort `build_sets`.

**The unscoreable expected ids are real.** With a non-numeric suffix such as ENG-642317-DECISION-..., the compare question gets no matching due date (due is keyed by the full string). `not_reproduced` marks it bad and drops it. That path is harmless. person_first and action_owner_issues are different: they keep the full string in `expected.ids`, it reproduces in the small set, and `ids_in` (KEY_RE) can only ever return 'ENG-39185' and the like, or nothing for 8+ digit keys.

**How often it happens.** I ran draw() plus the build_sets question logic, writing nothing, for 31 seeds (101-131, never 53/54):
- **Seed 115:** a picked, kept person_first question expects 'ENG-39185-ACCESS-CERTIFICATES-RETENTION-SCHEDULER'. The best possible own_score is 0.0, for every arm in both banks.
- **Seed 103:** a picked action_owner_issues question includes 'ENG-642317-DECISION-MESH-SCHEMA-REFACTOR'. The best possible F1 is 0.75.
- **Seed 119:** a compare_two question named an odd key and was dropped by `not_reproduced`, which is harmless.
- **Seed 106:** the draw included PM-31415926, but it appeared only in a set-aside question.

So about 2 draws in 31 (about 6%) give a picked question that cannot be scored correctly. The crash needs one of the four 8+ digit Linear documents to be drawn (about 1 draw in 31) and placed in one of the 8 compare pairs (7-8 of which get picked). I estimate that at well under 1% per draw.

**Effect on the test.** The bad question scores the same in both banks, so the size-difference rules are unaffected. It lowers the absolute level by about 0.015 (person_first) or 0.004 (action_owner) for every arm. That bears on rule 2 (v13 ≥ 0.92), but only at the margin. The fix is cheap and the set is not drawn yet: skip non-plain tracker keys in draw() and count them under their own skipped reason, and/or guard the unpacking in not_reproduced. Fixing it before freezing costs nothing in fairness.

The probe scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/rev5ka/ (odd_keys.py, collide.py, e2e.py, freq.py, s106.py).

findings.title: The hash-seed check reruns only the asking step; the bank's alias resolution happens at build time and is not checked
findings.evidence: run_5k.sh builds both banks once under PYTHONHASHSEED=0, then reruns only `ask ... --name factbank_v13_seed1` under seed 1. bank.resolve (bank.py:223) builds alias_doc from the set b.aliases, so which document a colliding alias points to is fixed at build time by the seed-0 iteration order. understand.json found the seed effect exactly here: answers flipped only after the bank was rebuilt under another seed. The draw removes ticket and PR collisions (0 in throwaway sets 997, 101 and 202), but 33, 21 and 28 'id:' aliases per set still belong to more than one document. A seed-1 check that skips the build cannot see that dependence, even though the pre-registration's reason for fixing the seed is 'which entity a colliding name resolves to can depend on it'.
findings.fix: Also build the 5,000-document bank under PYTHONHASHSEED=1 (into a separate folder) and run v13 against it. Or state in the pre-registration that the check covers the asking step only, with the build fixed at seed 0.

verdict.reason: The facts the reviewer cites are correct. run_5k.sh reruns only `ask` under PYTHONHASHSEED=1. bank.resolve (bank.py:223) builds alias_doc from a set. Each throwaway set has 33, 21 and 28 colliding 'id:' aliases. But the conclusion doesn't follow, because those collisions never reach resolve's output. resolve only rewrites a fact's entity or value_entity when it is 'key:<alias>', so set order matters only for a colliding alias that some 'key:' fact points to. I checked that in the throwaway draws in rev5ka (big7, big101, big202), using scripts under rev5ka/hsc. (1) No colliding alias is referenced by any 'key:' fact in any of the three sets. The colliding ones are deal IDs on Gmail and Fireflies documents (id:deal-*, id:acme-*, id:crm-*). The only references that produce 'key:id:' come from linked_gmail_threads, linked_fireflies and related_incident_id, and none of them matches any document alias at all (0 of 402 in big7). (2) I built the full in-memory bank under PYTHONHASHSEED=0 and again under 1, then hashed sources, entities, texts, sorted aliases and every fact row. The hashes are identical for big202 and big7, for both the plain bank and the --text-facts bank (big202 32f78b69…/796276b7…, big7 fbe45684…/17f7b997…). The rest of build() inserts in fixed order, with aliases sorted. (3) On the unfiltered 5,089-document mt5k there are 38 colliding aliases. Only 5 are referenced (eng-314159, eng-4821, eng-4829, sup-18421, sup-4821), and all are ticket keys, which the draw removes ('ticket key already drawn'). None of the 22 colliding id aliases there is referenced either. So the build-time seed effect found in understand.json comes only from reused ticket keys, which the draw rules out, and the bank comes out the same under either seed. Rebuilding under seed 1 would almost surely show nothing new. The ask-time rerun covers the part that can still depend on the seed: FactBank.named returns every copy of an alias. At most the pre-registration could say the check covers the asking step, which is a matter of wording, not a defect.

findings.title: If the set-aside folder gets no questions, the script stops before the hash-seed check and the score
findings.evidence: _write_set writes an empty questions.jsonl for $X when aside_picked is empty. Both asks then write 0-byte answer files: factbank_test.ask and ask_plans call _write_jsonl even with no rows. So `test -s $X/factbank.jsonl` fails at run_5k.sh:39, the script prints "missing factbank in ...x" and exits 1. Lines 44-45 (the hash-seed check and `score`) never run, even though every deciding answer for BIG and SMALL is already on disk. I counted set-aside questions on 11 other seeds against the real remaining pool, writing only under rev5ka/: 30, 21, 6, 14, 15, 13, 32, 15, 33, 18, 28. The minimum is 6, so zero is unlikely but possible. Every non-empty case runs fine. With the duplicate filter, the 'named' and 'answer' reasons were always empty and only 'tickets' was left.
findings.fix: In the loop, run the X folder only when `test -s $X/questions.jsonl`, or loosen its output check to `[ -s $X/questions.jsonl ] || continue`. _lenient already copes with 0 questions.

verdict.reason: The failure is real, but it will almost never happen. I reproduced it: I copied the mdord banks into rev5ka/xsim0, gave it an empty questions.jsonl, and ran the X-folder part of the loop exactly as run_5k.sh lines 29-41 have it. Every arm exited 0 but wrote a 0-byte answer file, because factbank_test.ask and factbank_multi.ask_plans call _write_jsonl even when there are no rows. `test -s` then printed "missing factbank in .../xsim0" and the script exited 1 before the lines that would have run the hash-seed check and `score` (44-45). The scorer itself copes with the empty folder: _lenient returned questions=0 and None scores without error. The X folder is empty only if no question at all is set aside, since pick(aside) is empty only when aside is empty. With the duplicate filter, only the 'tickets' reason fires. Every person who has 2-4 Linear issues and at least one Jira ticket in the set yields a person_count question that is always set aside, because the Jira tickets change the count. So 0 set-aside questions requires that no such person exists. I loaded all Linear (20,923) and Jira (3,588) documents in the remaining pool. 501 people are assignees in both. I then sampled the draw's targets (341 Linear, 59 Jira) 20,000 times, ignoring the duplicate filter. On average 7.9 people qualify, and none qualified in 1 of 20,000 draws (about 5e-5). The other reviewer's draws for seeds 7, 101 and 202 (30, 21 and 6 set-aside questions) agree with this. If it did happen, it would change no number or verdict. BIG and SMALL are fully answered, and both banks are built, before the X iteration starts. The two skipped lines could be run by hand with the same result, and the set-aside report is information only. The fix is still trivial: skip X when its questions.jsonl is empty.

findings.title: The script never checks Ollama, which v12 needs for every new question
findings.evidence: form_md5k.jsonl and form_md5kx.jsonl do not exist yet; the dry run's form caches were deleted. So v12 calls Ollama for all 50 questions on BIG and up to 50 on X. Right now Ollama is up: the ollama serve process was started from the scratchpad at 06:45. llama3.2:3b digest a80c4f17 is loaded, the form prompt's fingerprint is bf3f84a670bd43be as frozen, and no_proxy covers 127.0.0.1 so urllib skips the agent proxy. One test form took 19.6 s with another job using a core, against Former's 600 s timeout. A cold load or the dry run's worst case (v12 max 58.8 s per question) is still well inside the timeout. But if the container restarts before the run, nothing restarts Ollama. v12 then fails on its first question and the subshell's set -e skips v14. The failure only shows up at the output check after BIG's ~19 minutes of other arms. It is not silent, and a rerun redraws the same set, but the time is lost.
findings.fix: Add a check before the draw: `curl -sf -m 5 127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags | grep -q a80c4f17 || { echo 'start ollama'; exit 1; }`.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. Every claim checks out.
- run_5k.sh has no Ollama check anywhere.
- $S/plan9/forms holds no form_md5k*.jsonl or form_dry5k* cache, so v12 must call the model for every new question.
- Former.form in cie/src/cie/factbank/reader.py calls urllib urlopen against OLLAMA_HOST (default 127.0.0.1:11434) with a 600 s timeout. There is no try/except and no fallback, and ask_plans has none either, so a refused connection crashes the process on the first question.
- ask_plans writes factbank_v12.jsonl only at the end through _write_jsonl. A crash leaves no file.
- I checked bash's behaviour with a small script. The background subshell inherits set -e, so v14 is skipped. A bare `wait` returns 0. The failure surfaces only at the `test -s ... || exit 1` check, after the other arms on BIG have finished.
- Ollama is up now: llama3.2:3b has digest a80c4f17, form_fingerprint() is bf3f84a670bd43be, and no_proxy covers 127.0.0.1. But it runs from the scratchpad binary, which is not on PATH. It is detached (PPID 1) and was started at 06:45, while the container booted at 05:18. So it was started by hand after a container start, and nothing restarts it automatically. No .claude hooks exist.

It does not affect the test:
- The failure is loud (exit 1).
- draw() uses mkdir(exist_ok=True) with fixed seeds, so a rerun produces the same set.
- The form cache is appended one question at a time and is deterministic (temperature 0, seed 0). Forms cached before a crash are the same ones a rerun would produce.
- The only side effect besides lost time is duplicate lines in peak.jsonl, which peak.py appends to. scale_test does not read that file, and it feeds no verdict.

The proposed curl check works as written.

findings.title: Time per question for v12 and v14 is skewed by how the arms are scheduled, and peak memory never reaches the report
findings.evidence: v4, v8, v9, v11 and v13 run 6-wide with v1, while v14 runs after v12 in the same subshell, mostly after the others have finished. In dry_run.json, v14's median at 5,089 documents is 4,257 ms against v13's 11,763 ms, with the same plan lessons apart from the form. v12's times on the big bank include the first-time model call (p90 49,667 ms). On the small bank v12 reads the cached forms (median 459 ms), so its big-vs-small time difference is not like for like. The v12 and v14 subshell and the seed-1 run are not wrapped in peak.py. scale_test never reads peak.jsonl, so the 'peak memory' promised under 'Also reported' is not in scale_report. A job from another review is using a core right now (rev5kb chance_cmp.py at 99% CPU), and part A's script has no idle-machine guard; part B's script asks for an idle machine. None of this touches the scores.
findings.fix: Either say in the pre-registration that the v12/v14 times include model calls (big bank only) and are measured under different contention, or run v12/v14 under peak.py and report times from the model-free arms only. Add peak.jsonl to scale_report, or say it is reported by hand. Start the run only on an idle machine.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. Every part of it checks out in the code.

1. **v12's 5k time includes the model calls; its small-bank time does not.** In factbank_multi.ask_plans, the timer starts on line 521, before former.form() on line 523. Former.form (reader.py) calls the local model with _ask() whenever the question is not in the cache. run_5k.sh runs the folders in the order BIG, SMALL, X and gives BIG and SMALL the same form file. build_sets writes the same picked questions to both folders, and form_md5k.jsonl does not exist yet. So v12 on BIG fills the cache with timed model calls, and v12 and v14 on SMALL only read it. The model is a local llama-server on the same 4 cores (PID 7239, about 50 CPU-minutes since the dry run started), so it also slows the other arms. This fits dry_run.json: v12 at 5k has p90 49,667 ms and max 58,845 ms, against v13's 17,898 ms p90.
2. **v14 is timed under less contention than the arms it is compared with.** v14 runs after v12 in one subshell, while v1 and v4/v8/v9/v11/v13 run side by side. In the dry run v14 had a median of 4,257 ms against v13's 11,763 ms at 5k, and 213 ms against 445 ms on the small bank.
3. **Peak memory is not measured for v12, v14 or the seed-1 run, and never reaches the report.** The v12/v14 subshell and the seed-1 run are not wrapped in peak.py. scale_test reads the answer files and *_build.json (seconds, bytes) but never reads peak.jsonl, so scale_report has no peak memory. The pre-registration still lists peak memory under "Also reported".
4. **Part A has no idle-machine check.** Part B only asks for one in a comment (run_5k_b.sh line 2 and its pre-registration). It does not enforce it either.

**Why it does not matter for the test:**
- Timing and memory are in "Also reported" only. No rule, score or verdict uses them; scale_test's rules read only the answers.
- Known limits already says the times were measured on a shared machine with several arms running at once.
- Each row records form.model_ms, so the model time can be stated or taken out of v12's 5k times after the run.
- Peak memory for the wrapped commands can be reported by hand from peak.jsonl.

A one-line note in the pre-registration, or wrapping the v12/v14 subshell in peak.py, would be a cheap improvement. It would not change any number the test decides on.

findings.title: Rule 1's 0.05 margin is smaller than one person or one planted pair: the questions cluster across kinds, and the 'tickets' set-aside makes it worse
findings.evidence:
I used the non-test draws already in scratchpad/rev5ka (seeds 7, 101 and 202, written by the parallel review). I grouped the picked questions by shared gold documents. In seed 101, one action-item owner carries 5 of the 21 combine questions: action_owner_issues-063, -095, -096 and -105, plus person_count-003. That is 5/21/3 = 0.079 of the three-group mean. One person failing at 5,000 would therefore break rule 1 (0.05) on their own and use up nearly all of rule 2's headroom below 1.000. In seed 7, two people carry 3 combine questions each.

The link group behaves the same way. In each draw, 13 or 14 of its 21 questions come from just 8 or 9 planted PR/issue pairs. Each pair is asked twice (pr_issue and issue_pr_author), so one pair is worth 0.032.

The set-aside drives part of this. In seed 101, 'tickets' set aside 12 of the 19 action items. pick() then had to take all 7 that were left, so the 4 items of one owner all went in. pick()'s preference for new things only works within a kind (_target is the kind plus the gold documents). The pre-registration's 'How to read differences' gives only per-question weights (0.015–0.04). 'Known limits' says only that questions share documents.
findings.fix: Before freezing, do one of two things. Either make pick() prefer people and PR/issue pairs that have not been asked about yet across all kinds, or cap the questions per entity. Or keep pick() and add the per-entity weight to 'How to read differences', and report the changed questions grouped by person or pair.

verdict.reason:
Only part of this holds up, and none of it changes a number or a verdict.

What I confirmed:
- In rev5ka/big101, one owner (Maya Patel) carries 5 of the 21 combine questions: action_owner_issues-063, -095, -096, -105 and person_count-003. That is 5/21/3 = 0.079 of the mean. The 'tickets' set-aside left 7 of 19 action items, and pick() took all 7.
- pick() prefers unasked things only within a kind: `seen` is reset per kind and `_target` includes the kind. So clusters that span kinds are not prevented.
- I re-ran questions() and pick() on the three rev5ka document sets with question seeds 1–8 (not 54). The largest one-person share of the mean ranged from 0.030 to 0.095. It was above 0.05 in 11 of 24 runs: all 8 on the big101 documents, 3 on big202, none on big7. So the real draw could well put one person above the margin.
- 'How to read differences' gives only per-question weights.

What I refuted:
1. 'Smaller than one planted pair' is wrong. In every draw a link cluster is at most 2 questions, 2/21/3 = 0.032, which is below 0.05.
2. A person with 3 questions weighs 0.045–0.048, also below 0.05. Only an outlier person of 4 to 6 questions crosses it.
3. The weighting does not bias the test. The control asks identical questions with identical expected answers. v13 is deterministic with the hash seed fixed. If one person's 4 to 6 questions fail at 5,000 and pass on the small bank, that is a genuine loss to size. Rule 1 failing would then be the correct verdict, and it already requires each worsened question to be diagnosed. Clustering changes how much of a real effect gets counted. It cannot fail rule 1 when no question is affected.
4. The problem is not new to this design; earlier tests had it worse. I grouped questions by shared non-meeting gold documents in the earlier 50-document held-out sets (mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdplan, mdrep, mdtick, mdord). Their largest combine clusters were 3–8 questions (up to 0.107 of the mean) and their largest link clusters 2–11 (up to 0.193). Those sets carried the same −0.05 margins, and rule 2's 0.969 baseline comes from them. The 5k pick() is less clustered than they were.
5. 'Known limits' already says the questions share documents and are fewer than 50 independent checks.

What is left is a reporting improvement, not a defect that matters: add the per-person weight to 'How to read differences', and group the changed questions by person in the report.

findings.title: Rules 3, 4 and 5 have no consequence in 'What decides', and rule 5 failed in the dry run
findings.evidence:
'What decides' uses only rules 1 and 2: 'It holds at 5,000 if rules 1 and 2 are both met'. Rule 4 is explicitly 'not a separate confirmation'. Rules 3 (the planner's lead) and 5 (right for the right reason) are not given any outcome at all.

In dry_run.json, rule 5 failed: v13's reason share was 0.979 on the small bank and 0.917 at 5,089 documents, a drop of 0.062. If the test meets rules 1 and 2 but not rule 5, the verdict would still read 'holds at 5,000', even though more of the right answers came from the wrong plan. That leaves room to interpret the result after the fact.
findings.fix: State what a failure of rule 3 and of rule 5 means for the verdict (for example: 'holds, but more answers are right for the wrong reason; each one is diagnosed'). Otherwise, move them from 'Rules' to 'Also reported'.

verdict.reason:
The finding is correct as a description, but it overstates the risk.

What I confirmed in cie/docs/FACTBANK_5K_PREREGISTRATION.md: 'What decides' (lines 106-110) uses only rules 1 and 2 ('It holds at 5,000 if rules 1 and 2 are both met'). Rule 4 is called 'not a separate confirmation'. Rules 3 and 5 get no outcome anywhere. The sister document, FACTBANK_5K_B_PREREGISTRATION.md line 95, does give its rules 3 and 5 a role ('Rules 3 and 5 say whether its own answers hold'). Part A has no matching line, so this looks like an omission rather than a choice.

The dry-run numbers are right. In docs/benchmarks/factbank_5k/dry_run.json, by_arm.reason_small.v13.mean is 0.979 and reason_5k.v13.mean is 0.917, a drop of 0.062. Rule 5 is false there, and so is rule 4. The pre-registration's dry-run section only mentions that rule 1 failed.

Why it does not change the test:
(1) The verdict is fixed mechanically by rules 1 and 2, so it cannot be reinterpreted later.
(2) scale_test (factbank_5k.py lines 359-367) computes all five rules, and to_markdown prints each as met or not met. A rule 5 failure would show in the report either way.
(3) The repo does this routinely. FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION decides on rules 1 and 2 and gives rules 4-7 no outcome. FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS reported a non-deciding rule 4 as 'not met' and explained it in the write-up.
(4) The dry-run failure does not show the finding's scenario ('right answers from the wrong plan'). 'Right for the right reason' means wholly right and the plan read every fact the answer rests on (factbank_multi.py line 598), so it can never exceed the plain score. The 0.062 drop in reason share matches the 0.063 drop in the plain score: link 0.938 to 0.75, the same three 'status email' due-date questions that broke rule 1. No right answer lost its right reason.

The scenario the finding worries about (rules 1 and 2 met, rule 5 not) is possible: two lost answers plus one answer right for the wrong reason would do it, since one question moves the mean by about 0.02. Only then would the meaning of rule 5 be left to the write-up.

So this is a low-severity gap in how the result reads, not in the verdict, the numbers or the scoring. A one-line fix before freezing would close it, for example matching Part B: 'Rules 3 and 5 say whether the planner's lead and its reasons hold; a failure is diagnosed question by question and does not change the verdict.' It cannot be added once the document is frozen.

findings.title: The 'status email' disclosure describes mt5k, not this draw: the extra documents almost never mention a question's ticket or PR
findings.evidence:
The pre-registration says 'at 5,000 there are Gmail documents about the ticket', and gives that as the cause of the dry run's three losses. I checked the three non-test draws:
- None of the 21 pr_issue tickets, and none of the PR numbers, is mentioned by any Gmail, Slack, Drive, Confluence, HubSpot or Fireflies document in the 5,000.
- Seed 101 drew the email wording twice (pr_issue-due_date-082 and -090), and neither ticket had a Gmail document about it.
- Across all 100 questions picked in seeds 7 and 101, the only documents outside the gold set that mention a question's keys or PR numbers are 42 other Linear issues.

The dry-run loss came from mt5k, which was built around the memory test's gold and linked documents (183 Jira against 59 in a draw). Keeping the wording is fair, because both banks get identical questions. But 'the test set may or may not draw that wording' leaves out the second condition, and the dry run's rule-1 failure does not predict the test.

Not checked, because it would need a 5,000-document bank: whether the planner can still reach Gmail by another path, such as PR → author → mailbox_owner_of. People asked about are named in a median of 8 to 15 other documents, including Gmail.
findings.fix: Correct the sentence in 'What size can still break'. Say that a plain draw rarely includes Gmail documents about a planted ticket. Also say that for the ticket-anchored questions (link and compare, about 28 of 50), the extra documents add only other Linear issues.

verdict.reason:
The finding is right about a detail but wrong about what follows from it. A plain draw seldom holds a Gmail document about a planted ticket. But the hazard does not need one, and it still fires in a plain draw.

How the planner reaches Gmail: bank links come only from structured fields (bank.add_document). In plans.check, rule 2 (other_system) keeps every plan that ends in the system the question names. It runs before rule 4 (kind of answer), and a rule is skipped only when no plan passes it. So for a question that starts at a PR and contains "email", any plan from the PR that ends in a Gmail document wins. The route can go through people (PR → reviewers or author → mailbox_owner_of or participants_internal_of). It does not have to go through the ticket.

What I checked, without building any 5,000-document bank (probe in rev5ka/emailprobe):
1. **A field-level reach probe** over the non-test draws already in rev5ka (seeds 7, 101 and 202). Within 2 hops, 74 of 77, 71 of 77 and 71 of 77 PRs reach Gmail. The first hop is the reviewers for 62 to 68 of them, the author for 29 to 42, and linked_linear for only 0 to 2. Seed 101's two email-wording questions show the same pattern: PR #19397 reaches 340 Gmail documents and PR #1080 reaches 296 (counted by path, 269 different documents in all), all through the reviewers. None of the 269 mentions either ticket key or PR number, which agrees with the finding's own check. mt5k is similar: 136 of 141 PRs reach Gmail, 120 of them through the reviewers and only 12 through linked_linear.
2. **A direct test with frozen v13.** I made two small banks for seed 101's two email-wording questions. The control is the 79-document small set; the second is the same set plus only those 269 Gmail documents. On the control, v13 answers both questions right (2025-02-14 and 2025-03-01). With the Gmail documents added, both are wrong: the plan is "→ reviewers → mailbox_owner_of [gmail] → first_email_at → earliest", and the answers are email subjects.

So the dry run's rule-1 loss does predict the test whenever this wording is drawn. Seed 101 drew it twice, which is about 0.03 to 0.04 of the mean against the 0.05 margin.

The proposed fix would mislead. It would say the extra documents add only other Linear issues to the questions that start from a ticket or PR, but these PRs reach hundreds of Gmail, Slack and Drive documents through people. The real flaw is small: the phrase "Gmail documents about the ticket" names the wrong route. A precise sentence would say Gmail documents reachable from the pull request through its reviewers and author, which makes the disclosure stronger, not weaker. That wording change alters no number, verdict or fairness, since both banks get identical questions.

findings.title: The hash-seed check re-runs only the ask, but the documented dependence happens when the bank is built
findings.evidence:
run_5k.sh runs `PYTHONHASHSEED=1 ... factbank_multi ask --work $BIG ... --name factbank_v13_seed1` against factbank_v2.sqlite, which was built under seed 0. The dependence the investigation found is in bank.resolve (bank.py:221), which build() calls at line 242. It builds alias_doc from a set, so which copy of a shared alias wins is fixed when the bank is built and stored.

So 'The hash-seed check changed no answer' (dry run) cannot speak to that mechanism. The draw's key and PR-number dedupe removes most collisions, but alias collisions on 'id:' values remain (33 in the seed-997 probe).
findings.fix: Rebuild factbank_v2 under PYTHONHASHSEED=1 in a separate folder (about 115 MB) and ask v13 there. Otherwise, describe the check as covering only Python's string hashing during asking.

verdict.reason:
One part of the finding is true. run_5k.sh asks v13 again under PYTHONHASHSEED=1 against factbank_v2.sqlite, which was built under seed 0. bank.resolve (bank.py:221-230) builds alias_doc from the set b.aliases, and build() stores the result. So the seed-1 run does not repeat that build step.

The impact the finding claims does not survive a check. resolve's set order only matters for an alias that points to more than one document AND that some key: fact or entity uses. I wrote a probe, rev5ka/refute_hs/p.py. It runs add_document with text_facts=True and then resolve, exactly as the v2 build does. It then hashes the whole built bank: sources, entities, texts, sorted aliases and fact rows. I ran it under seeds 0 and 1 on three drawn 5,000-document sets (seeds 7, 101 and 202, made by draw()).
- **Shared aliases remain:** 33, 21 and 28. They are all 'id:' values: deal ids on Gmail messages, one shared meeting id on Fireflies, and similar.
- **None of them is used by any key: fact or entity**, so resolve never has to choose a copy for them.
- **The banks are identical under both seeds:** 17f7b997…, b440ffe7… and 796276b7… (outputs in rev5ka/refute_hs/*.json).
- **Same on the undeduped mt5k:** an earlier probe (rev5ka/hsc/mt5k_s0.json) found 22 shared 'id:' aliases, none used. Only ticket keys were used there, and the draw removes those.

So once the draw has removed repeated keys and PR numbers, building the bank does not depend on the hash seed. Asking again under seed 1 on the seed-0 bank then tests the only place left where the seed can matter, which is asking. The proposed rebuild under seed 1 would give the same bank.

The pre-registration describes the check accurately: "v13 is run again on the 5,000-document bank with seed 1". All decisive runs fix seed 0 anyway. The dry-run line refers to mt5k, a seen set that gives no results, and its 50 kept questions had already been filtered to exclude repeated keys. No number, verdict or fairness point changes.

findings.title: Items promised in 'Also reported' that scale_test does not compute
findings.evidence:
- **Peak memory:** peak.py writes peak.jsonl, but scale_test never reads it. The v12 and v14 asks and the seed-1 ask are not wrapped by peak.py, so they have no memory figure at all.
- **Comparison with the 50-document tests:** 'each arm against the 50-document tests (order test, and the eight-set mean)' is not computed anywhere in factbank_5k.py.
- **Hash-seed check:** the pre-registration says 'every changed answer is reported', but hashseed_check stores only the ids of changed questions, not the answers.
findings.fix: Read peak.jsonl into scale_report and wrap the v12, v14 and seed-1 asks in peak.py. Add the 50-document reference numbers, or say they are copied by hand from FACTBANK_ORDER_RESULTS.md. Store both answers for each changed question.

verdict.reason:
The code facts are accurate, but none of the three is a protocol defect. The pre-registration lists these items under "Also reported" for the hand-written FACTBANK_5K_RESULTS.md. It never says scale_test must compute them, and every promised item can still be reported from what the run keeps.

1. Peak memory. It is true that factbank_5k.py never reads peak.jsonl (a grep for "peak" finds nothing). It is also true that run_5k.sh does not wrap the v12/v14 subshell or the PYTHONHASHSEED=1 ask in peak.py. But the promise reads "the build times, storage and peak memory", with no "for each arm". peak.py does record every build, plus the v1, v4, v8, v9, v11 and v13 asks, in peak.jsonl in each work folder, and that file is kept. v12 and v14 load the same bank and lessons as v11 and v13, so their Python process would use about the same memory. A per-arm memory figure was never promised, so nothing promised is missing.

2. Comparison with the 50-document tests. These are fixed reference numbers from earlier tests. FACTBANK_ORDER_RESULTS.md line 34 holds v13 0.969 and v14 0.982, and factbank_5k.py already hard-codes 0.969 as the basis of LEVEL. Copying them into the results doc by hand matches how earlier results docs were written. No code is needed, and no rule depends on it.

3. Hash-seed check. hashseed_check stores only the ids of changed questions. Both answer files, factbank_v13.jsonl and factbank_v13_seed1.jsonl, stay in the 5,000-document folder, so every changed answer can still be reported. In the dry run nothing changed.

No rule (1 to 5), verdict or test number depends on any of these. At most, wrapping the v12, v14 and seed-1 asks in peak.py would be a small nicety.

findings.title: Rule 2's 0.92 uses a weaker reference than this test's own wordings, and calls known sets 'held-out'
findings.evidence:
The arithmetic checks out: 0.969 − 0.05 = 0.919. 0.969 is v13's mean over mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdplan, mdrep and mdtick. FACTBANK_ORDER_RESULTS.md lists that number as 'earlier sets (guard, known)'.

Those sets used other wordings, including mdwords, a deliberately unfamiliar-words set where v13 scored 0.877. This test reuses the order test's wordings, on which v13 scored 1.000 at 50 documents. A same-wording reference gives 0.95, and the dry run's 0.937 would fail that.

0.92 was fixed before the dry run (commit 3e8fc28 comes before ff376a1), so it was not tuned to it. Rule 2 only matters when the small bank scores below 0.97.
findings.fix: Explain why the eight-set mean is the reference rather than the same-wording order test (1.000 → 0.95), or switch to the same-wording reference. Call the eight sets 'known' rather than 'held-out'.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the main claim. One part of it is weak.

Confirmed from the repository:
- **The arithmetic.** v13's eight-set values in `docs/benchmarks/factbank_order/order_report.json` average 0.9685, and 0.9685 − 0.05 = 0.9185. `LEVEL = 0.92` is set in `cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_5k.py` line 46.
- **mdwords is in the mean.** It is the deliberately unfamiliar-words set, and v13 scored 0.877 on it. Without mdwords the mean is 0.982, which gives 0.932.
- **The same wordings scored 1.000 for v13.** That was the order test. The dry run's small bank on mt5k also scored 1.000.
- **The project's own design note proposed 0.95.** `docs/benchmarks/factbank_5k/understand.json` (committed in 3e8fc28 with the draft) says: "R2, level: v13(5k) ≥ 0.95, within 0.05 of the order test's 1.000, the form of the replication's level check."
- **The replication used a same-wording reference.** `docs/FACTBANK_PLAN_REPLICATION.md` rule 2 is "within 0.05 of the first test's 0.975". The 5K pre-registration cites the replication as its model for reusing wordings.
- **The switch to the eight-set mean is not explained.** The pre-registration changes to 0.92 without giving a reason.
- **0.92 was not tuned to the dry run.** It is already in 3e8fc28 (06:51). The dry-run banks were built at 06:49, but answering finished only at 07:08.

What I could refute or limit:
- **'held-out' is not wrong.** It is the project's standing term for these sets. The order and ticket pre-registrations both say "the mean of the eight/seven earlier held-out sets". The sets were held out from training and are also known now, so both words are accurate. This half of the finding is a wording preference.
- **The eight-set mean is a defensible choice.** It averages 8 draws across documents and kind mixes. The order test's own results call its 1.000 narrow, with easy wordings. With the 5K pick (7 compare questions in their own group), a single compare error costs about 0.048. A threshold of 0.95 would therefore allow about one error.

So the issue is real but low: a reference choice that departs from the project's own proposal and precedent and is not explained.

It does not matter for the test:
- **The threshold was fixed before any result was seen.**
- **Rule 2 can only change the verdict in a narrow case:** rule 1 is met, the small bank scores below 1.000, and the 5,000-document score falls between 0.92 and 0.95. If the small bank scores 1.000, as both same-wording runs did, rule 1 already requires at least 0.95, so the choice of rule 2 threshold makes no difference.
- **Rule 1 decides size either way.** In that case only the label changes, from 'holds' to 'harder for another reason'.
- **The minimal fix changes no number:** a sentence explaining the choice, plus noting the sets are known.

findings.title: 'Jira tickets have no due date' is inaccurate
findings.evidence:
In 1,500 lexsample Jira records, due_date is never set. But sla_due_at is set on 1,155 and first_response_due_at on 878. The bank treats *_at fields as dates (bank.py:103). Under the Linear-plus-Jira reading, a ticket whose SLA is due first is a defensible answer to 'which one is due first'. ticket_reading only checks due_date.

The impact is small. In the non-test draws, 0 or 1 picked person_first question per draw is about a Jira holder, and none of those people has a Jira SLA date earlier than their first Linear due date.
findings.fix: Reword the sentence (for example, 'Jira tickets have no due_date field; their SLA dates are not counted'). Alternatively, have ticket_reading also flag person_first questions where a Jira sla_due_at comes before the Linear first due date.

verdict.reason: The prose claim is wrong, but fixing it would not change any number. FACTBANK_5K_PREREGISTRATION.md lines 64-65 say "Which is due first" never changes "because Jira tickets have no due date". The data says otherwise. Of 6,120 Jira records, sla_due_at is set on 4,668 and first_response_due_at on 3,632. One record, INT-33210 (assignee Victor Chen, due_date 2026-03-22), even has a literal due_date, and it is still in the remaining pool. In the excluded lexsample set, 1,793 of 2,342 Jira records have sla_due_at and none has due_date. The test wordings say "Of all the tickets assigned to {p}, which one is due first?" with no tracker named (factbank_order/wordings.json). So under the Linear-plus-Jira reading, a Jira ticket whose SLA comes due first is a defensible answer. ticket_reading (factbank_5k.py:179) compares only due_date. It does read due_date on Jira too, so the code is right about INT-33210; only the sentence is wrong. The finding's impact estimate is a little too low. In my non-test draw with seed 31 / qseed 32, 3 of the 8 picked person_first questions were about Jira holders. One of them, about Ethan Park, has a Jira SLA (SUP-8675309, 2026-03-11) before his first Linear due date (ENG-982733, 2026-03-20). Draws 41, 61, 71, 83, 97 and 113, plus the reviewer's 101, 202 and 997, picked no such question. That is about 1 in 10 draws. It still does not move a score. In the reviewer's probe bank (rev5ka/pfprobe), the Jira SLA facts were present for all 5 SLA-earlier cases. Every arm checked (v4, v8, v9, v11, v13) planned "assignee_of -> due_date -> earliest" and never used sla_due_at. engine.py also maps the word "due" only to due_date. So a question like this, if picked, is answered with the Linear-only key and scored the same either way. Rewording the sentence is the right fix; the strict/lenient scoring, rules and verdicts would not change.

findings.title: Planted pairs: 'no other pull request in the benchmark' is not what the code checks, and the pool is small and already probed
findings.evidence:
draw() builds refs from `linked`, which holds only the documents left after the exclusions. So the code checks for other referencing PRs among the remaining documents, not the whole benchmark. Of the 26 distinct planted issues in the seed 7, 101 and 202 draws, 10 are referenced by another PR in the excluded sets. This does not affect whether answers are unique within the set.

Only 56 pairs are eligible across the whole remaining pool. The review probes in rev5ka (seeds 7, 101, 202 and 997) have already planted 26 of them, and v13 and v4 were run on small7. Seed 53's 10 pairs will probably include about 4 or 5 pairs that have already been seen in review. The pre-registration says development used only mt5k.
findings.fix: Write 'that no other pull request left after the exclusions references', and give the size of the eligible pool (56). Disclose that review probes drew from the remaining pool with other seeds.

verdict.reason:
I checked both parts against the code and the probe outputs, and both hold.

(1) Wording. draw() in cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_5k.py builds `refs` from `linked`. `linked` is loaded only from by_src = remaining(index, exclude), so the check is "no other remaining pull request references K". The code's own docstring says this correctly ("no other pull request left in the benchmark"). The pre-registration (line 53) drops "left" and says "no other pull request in the benchmark references". I loaded the 3,315 excluded GitHub documents (rev5ka/refpf/excl_refs.py). Of the 26 distinct planted issues in the seed 7, 101 and 202 draws, exactly 10 have linked_linear references from excluded pull requests (ENG-19142, 5156, 12890, 5418, 8219, 8213, 4932, 12458, 9213, 3127). So the pre-registration's sentence is literally false. Answers inside the set stay unique, because the set is drawn only from the remaining documents that refs covers.

(2) Pool size and exposure. I rebuilt the candidate list from rev5ka/linked.pkl (rev5ka/refpf/cands.py). It has 56 candidates, every draw output reports planted_candidates=56, and the rebuilt shuffles match the saved planted lists for seeds 7, 101 and 202. Those three seeds plant 26 distinct pairs. Seed 997 raises this to 31, so the finding's "26 across four seeds" is a slight undercount. v13 and v4 answer files exist for all 50 questions in rev5ka/small7. The expected overlap for a fresh seed is 10 x 31/56, about 5.5 pairs (simulated over seeds 1000-2999: mean 5.6, at least 4 seen pairs in 93% of draws). I did not compute seed 53. The planted pairs supply most pull request questions (for seed 997, 10 of the 18 pr_issue questions drawn came from planted pairs). The pre-registration's Development section mentions only mt5k and the dry run, and says nothing about review draws from the remaining pool.

Why it does not matter for the test: both fixes are wording and disclosure. Leaving them out changes no draw, expected answer, score or verdict. The overlap with pairs seen in review exists whether or not it is disclosed. It would only bear on fairness if code or lessons were changed in response to the small7 results before freezing, and nothing shows that happened.

findings.title: v12's time per question is not comparable between the banks: its 5,000-document time includes the small model's calls
findings.evidence:
The `ms` field in ask_plans includes former.form(), which calls llama3.2:3b when the form cache misses. run_5k.sh shares one form cache (form_$PX.jsonl) between BIG and SMALL and runs BIG first. So v12 fills the cache with model calls on the 5,000-document bank, and on the small bank it only reads the cache.

In the dry run, v12 at 5,000 documents had a p90 of 49.7 s and a maximum of 58.8 s, against 17.9 s and 23.1 s for v13. On the small bank v12's p90 was 0.6 s. 'Time per question for each arm on both banks' would show this as an effect of size.
findings.fix: Fill the form cache before any timed run (for example, run v12 on SMALL first). Otherwise, state that v12's 5,000-document time includes the model's calls.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. The code backs every step of the finding.

(1) Timing includes the form call. In src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py, ask_plans starts `t = time.perf_counter()` before `former.form(q["question"])`, and the row's `ms` is measured from that point.

(2) A cache miss calls the model inside that window. Former.form in src/cie/factbank/reader.py calls `self._ask` (Ollama llama3.2:3b) when the key (question, prompt fingerprint) is not in the cache, then appends the result to the cache file.

(3) Both banks get the same question strings. build_sets in factbank_5k.py writes the same `picked` questions to BIG and SMALL. run_5k.sh gives both the cache form_$PX.jsonl and loops `for W in $BIG $SMALL $X`, so BIG runs first. form_md5k.jsonl does not exist yet in plan9/forms, so v12 on BIG misses for every question. v12 on SMALL, and v14 on BIG and SMALL, only read the cache.

(4) The reported time takes the raw value. `_ms()` in factbank_5k.py takes the median, p90 and max of `r["ms"]` with nothing subtracted, and fills `time_ms` for every arm on both banks. Neither the pre-registration ("Also reported", "Known limits") nor the report says that v12's 5,000-document time includes the model's calls.

(5) The dry run shows the effect. In dry_run.json, v12 at 5k has p90 49,667 ms and max 58,845 ms. Against that: v13 17,898 / 23,127, v11 17,409 / 23,227, and v14 at 5k (form-filtered, cache hits) 5,262 / 5,862. v12 on the small bank has p90 597 ms. v12 does the same form-filtered bank work as v14, so its extra tail matches model calls rather than bank work. The dry-run folders and form cache have been deleted, so I could not split model_ms row by row.

The finding is right, but its reach is limited. It affects only a reported timing number, not any rule (rules 1 to 5 use scores) or the decision. It also creates a second asymmetry the reviewer did not name: at 5k, v12's time includes the model calls but v14's does not. Running v12 on SMALL first, or warming the cache, would fix it. A caveat could also be added in the write-up after the run.
